title: Build a trading-pattern bot
about: An honest path from 'I have a hunch' to 'here's whether it actually works'. The hardest part of this isn't the code — it's not fooling yourself. Each step is small; do it before moving on.

steps.title: Pick one precise question
steps.what: Write a single sentence your bot will answer, e.g. 'When social-media fear about gold is unusually high, is gold's next-week return higher than usual?' Name the asset, the signal, and the horizon.
steps.why: A vague goal ('predict the market') can't be tested or disproven. A precise one can, and that's the whole game.
steps.hint: Put the sentence at the top of a new README.md. You'll be surprised how often writing it reveals you haven't decided something.
steps.say: What's the one question? Asset, signal, horizon. I'll wait — this is the most important step.

steps.title: Get the data and cache it
steps.what: Fetch two things: the price history of the asset, and the signal you're testing. Save them to a data/ folder so you never re-download while experimenting.
steps.why: Live-fetching inside your analysis makes runs slow and non-reproducible. Cache once; iterate forever.
steps.hint: A tiny function per source — fetch_prices(), fetch_signal() — each writing a CSV. Print the date range and row count so you can eyeball gaps.
steps.say: Prices and your signal, saved to disk. Small functions, one per source.

steps.title: Line the two up on dates — carefully
steps.what: Join signal and price by date. Decide exactly when each day's signal is KNOWN versus when you could act on it. A signal stamped at a day's close can only be traded the NEXT day.
steps.why: Look-ahead is the mistake that makes worthless strategies look brilliant. Almost every too-good backtest has it hiding here.
steps.hint: Add a one-day lag between signal and trade on purpose. Later, write a test that scrambles all future data and checks today's features don't change.
steps.say: This is the trap everyone falls in. A signal from today's close is tradable tomorrow, not today. Lag it.

steps.title: Turn the raw signal into a feature
steps.what: Raw numbers rarely compare across time. Make a feature that asks 'is this unusual?' — for example, today's value minus its trailing-year average, divided by its trailing-year spread (a z-score).
steps.why: A fear reading of 0.3 means nothing alone; 'highest in a year' means something. Normalising against the PAST (never the whole history) keeps it honest.
steps.hint: Use a rolling window that only looks backwards (pandas .rolling(...).mean() on data up to today). If you used the full history's mean, you just leaked the future again.
steps.say: Make it answer 'is this unusual versus its own recent past?' Backward-looking windows only.

steps.title: Define what you're predicting
steps.what: Create the target: the asset's return over your horizon, starting the day AFTER the signal. One column, clearly named, aligned to the day the signal was known.
steps.why: If the feature and target aren't aligned to the right days, everything downstream is measuring noise or cheating.
steps.hint: forward_return(t) = price(t + 1 + horizon) / price(t + 1) - 1. Print a few rows by hand and check the dates with a calendar.
steps.say: The thing you're predicting: the return AFTER you could have traded. Check three rows by hand.

steps.title: Does the feature relate to the target at all?
steps.what: Before any backtest, just measure the correlation between feature and forward return (the 'information coefficient'). Plot a scatter. Is it even faintly there?
steps.why: A backtest can turn pure noise into a pretty equity curve. A plain correlation can't lie as easily — it's your reality check.
steps.hint: Expect something tiny, like 0.02–0.05, if it's real at all. Huge correlations usually mean a bug or leakage, not a goldmine.
steps.say: Simplest honest test first: do the two even correlate? Small is normal. Huge is a bug.

steps.title: Backtest the honest way: walk forward
steps.what: Split time into chunks. Decide your rule using only PAST chunks, then trade the next chunk. Roll forward. Add a one-day execution lag and subtract realistic trading costs.
steps.why: Testing a rule on the same data you invented it on is how you fool yourself. Walk-forward is the closest cheap thing to 'would this have worked live?'
steps.hint: Re-fit each year using data before that year only. Keep a plain buy-and-hold curve next to yours — beating it is the real bar.
steps.say: Only ever trade on a rule built from the past. And always draw buy-and-hold beside you.

steps.title: Try to kill it: the placebo test
steps.what: Run your entire pipeline on shuffled or time-shifted signal data, many times. If your 'real' result isn't clearly better than these nonsense runs, you found nothing.
steps.why: This is what separates a signal from a coincidence. If random data does as well as yours, yours was random.
steps.hint: Shift the signal against prices by a random amount, re-run, record the Sharpe. Do it 200 times. Where does your real number fall in that pile?
steps.say: Now attack your own result. Feed it nonsense 200 times. Are you really above the noise?

steps.title: Decide — and be okay with 'no'
steps.what: Write up what you found in plain language, including the parts that didn't work. Decide: is this real enough to keep, or is the honest answer 'mostly noise'?
steps.why: 'It doesn't work' is a real, valuable result and most honest quant projects land there. Knowing WHY is the skill you were actually building.
steps.hint: If it's faint, the usual next move isn't a fancier model — it's more breadth: the same weak signal across hundreds of assets, not one.
steps.say: You built the thing. Whatever the answer, you can now tell truth from wishful thinking — that's the win.
